nodes.label: Kosmos Architecture
The kernel as the narrowest box
nodes.rationale: The textbook Unix diagram makes the kernel the widest box because a filesystem, a terminal and drawing are all kernel code. Kosmos inverts it: almost everything that picture puts inside the kernel is a process beside the shell rather than underneath it.

nodes.label: The eighteen syscalls
nodes.rationale: Four of them - endpoint, call, receive, reply - are the entire mechanism by which every service is reached. The rest is process lifetime, time, memory, and the two concessions the boot console forces (write, getchar). There is no open, because there is nothing for the kernel to open.

nodes.label: Capability index at the syscall boundary
nodes.rationale: Every syscall that names something takes a number meaningful only inside the calling process's own table. There is no global identifier for anything, anywhere, on purpose.

nodes.label: No global namespace
nodes.rationale: A process cannot walk a tree to find something because there is no tree to walk. A program that was not given /dev does not get permission denied - the path does not exist.

nodes.label: Statically declared kernel pools
nodes.rationale: 48 threads, 32 processes, 96 endpoints, 32 address spaces. Running out is an error at a known limit rather than a failure at an unknown one, and every number is reported by ps because a limit nothing counts is a limit nobody can find.

nodes.label: arch/aarch64 - which CPU are you
nodes.rationale: Page tables, exception vector, context switch, barriers. Not abstracted across architectures; a second architecture reimplements it rather than parameterising it.

nodes.label: hal/qemu-virt - which peripheral do you have
nodes.rationale: Deliberately eleven functions: the right shape for a HAL only becomes visible once there is a second real target, and writing it now with one target produces the shape of QEMU with generic names.

nodes.label: Drivers still linked into the kernel
nodes.rationale: Knowingly in the wrong place: the kernel needs a console before there is a userland to provide one, and the boot screen has to be drawn before init exists to draw it. The largest gap between the design diagram and the real one.

nodes.label: C at EL0 inside a process
nodes.rationale: gfx.c, stb_truetype, serialize.c and libc are compiled into the user image and run with the process's own page tables. A bug there can corrupt only the process it is in - the same blast radius as the Lua above it, only faster. The one qualification is a surface shared with the compositor, which is shared memory.

nodes.label: Tracing cat /bin/ls.lua across every boundary
nodes.rationale: Keypress, virtio-input interrupt, GIC, exception vector, kernel input ring, SYS_GETCHAR, the shell asking /bin, SYS_ENDPOINT and SYS_SPAWN, the runner fetching the program, cat's IPC read in 1400-byte chunks, the console server, SYS_WRITE, pixels.

nodes.label: The shell hands the name, not the bytes
nodes.rationale: The shell asked whether the file existed and handed the path to a process that could fetch it, so the bytes cross the boundary once. The first design sent the source in the spawn message and broke the moment a program grew past 2,048 bytes.

nodes.label: The window manager owns every pixel
nodes.rationale: Applications send lists of drawing commands; the wm owns the pixels, which is why a hung application still has a window that moves. wm hello-win,stuck is the standing demonstration and has a display check.

nodes.label: C vs Lua decided by blast radius
nodes.rationale: If a bug there can corrupt another process it is C's job to prevent; if it can only kill its own process it may be Lua.

nodes.label: No POSIX personality at system level
nodes.rationale: A libc inside an app is fine and necessary; fork, signals, global descriptors and a tree reachable without a namespace are forbidden. It means ports get patched rather than accommodated, and that is the deliberate price of the rest.

nodes.label: The runner
nodes.rationale: Receives the path rather than the source, builds a namespace from the capabilities it was handed, and fetches the program through it.

nodes.label: The console server
nodes.rationale: Printing is an IPC call to it; it alone calls SYS_WRITE, and the kernel console puts each byte on the UART and blits its glyph into the framebuffer.

nodes.label: One binary, many roles
nodes.rationale: The image carries a single userland ELF and the role number it is spawned with decides what it becomes. Since September 2026 user/init/main.c dispatches the server roles before the Lua interpreter is opened, so those processes have no collector at all rather than a promise not to allocate.

nodes.label: Pixel loops are the standing C exception
nodes.rationale: Lua decides what is drawn and where; the loop happens inside a surface, in C, and nothing in Lua ever computes a pixel offset - the pitch is not width * 4 and pretending it is produces diagonal lines.

nodes.label: The stale SMP-ready claim
nodes.rationale: This document still says the code is written SMP-ready with a per-CPU runqueue and TPIDR_EL1. docs/smp.md counts the same claim and finds none of the three has ever existed.

nodes.label: Boundaries testable from outside
nodes.rationale: A pitch bug in the graphics primitives passes 103 of 103 in-guest tests because every read and write agree with each other. It is only visible to an observer on the other side of the framebuffer, which is why the suite boots QEMU and inspects the scanned-out picture.

nodes.label: A process cannot be ended from outside
nodes.rationale: Control-C works by asking, so a program that polls can be stopped and /bin/spin.lua cannot. A real kill has to unlink the target from three IPC queues and settle what happens to whoever holds a reply handle.
